title: AI Agents Don’t Eliminate Management. They Change What We Manage.
description: Signal vs. Noise: Why the next wave of AI will test leadership, accountability, and the true meaning of productivity.
author: Jeffrey Cortez
html:
Signal vs. Noise

The next challenge in AI adoption isn’t getting machines to do more work. It’s learning how to lead when they do.

For years, we’ve been told that artificial intelligence would change how we work.

First, AI helped us find information. Then it began drafting emails, summarizing documents, generating code, and answering increasingly complex questions.

We called these tools assistants because that’s largely what they were. We asked a question, received an answer, and decided what to do next.

But something important is changing.

AI is moving beyond answering questions and toward executing work.

And while that sounds like a technological milestone, I believe it introduces a much bigger management challenge.

When software begins performing work instead of simply recommending it, who becomes responsible for the outcome?

That question deserves more attention than another prediction about which jobs AI might replace.

The Shift From Assistance to Execution

On October 28, at GitHub Universe 2026, GitHub introduced capabilities designed to coordinate AI agents across multiple projects, maintain their work across devices, and automate workflows that can propose improvements based on their results. Its accompanying release notes describe agents bringing results back for human review, with Copilot Projects in public preview.

These announcements reflect a broader direction in the industry.

Instead of asking an AI assistant to help write a piece of software, a developer can increasingly assign an objective and have agents work through multiple steps toward completing it.

Imagine extending that model beyond software development.

An agent might research prospective customers, prepare personalized outreach, analyze business performance, investigate operational problems, or draft changes to an internal process.

Another agent might review the work, identify potential problems, and recommend corrections.

A third could coordinate those activities and report progress.

The appeal is obvious.

More work can move forward without someone manually performing every step.

But there’s an important distinction between work being performed and work being completed correctly.

And that distinction is where leadership enters the picture.

We Are Creating a New Management Problem

Consider how we manage people.

When we delegate an assignment to an employee, we generally establish expectations, provide resources, define boundaries, and evaluate the results.

We don’t assume that assigning a task guarantees a successful outcome.

We also recognize that different employees require different levels of supervision depending on their experience, the complexity of the work, and the consequences of making a mistake.

Why would we approach AI agents differently?

An AI agent may be capable of operating continuously, processing substantial amounts of information, and completing tasks faster than a person.

But speed doesn’t necessarily mean sound judgment.

An agent might complete a technical assignment while overlooking a business requirement. It might produce a polished report based on incomplete information. It might successfully execute an instruction that was poorly conceived in the first place.

From the system’s perspective, the task may be complete.

From the organization’s perspective, the problem may have just begun.

The ability to execute a task is not the same as the authority to decide whether that task should be executed.

That distinction should be fundamental to how organizations deploy autonomous systems.

Agents are a new form of operational capacity—not independently accountable replacements for teams. That capacity still needs direction, controls, and human judgment.

The Lessons From Managing AI-Assisted Work

In my own work developing technology solutions and directing AI-assisted workflows, I’ve become increasingly interested in the relationship between delegation, verification, and accountability.

The appeal of delegating work to AI is undeniable.

You can distribute assignments across specialized capabilities. One system can focus on implementation, another on evaluating quality, and another on identifying potential issues.

But organizing work this way doesn’t eliminate the need for management.

It changes where management effort goes.

Instead of spending all your time directing every technical step, you begin spending more time establishing expectations, reviewing outcomes, coordinating dependencies, and deciding when intervention is necessary.

And that’s where an important lesson emerges:

An AI agent can report that a task is finished. That doesn’t mean the business objective has been achieved.

A functioning feature isn’t necessarily a useful feature.

A completed workflow isn’t necessarily a reliable workflow.

And a successful automated test doesn’t necessarily mean the result is ready for customers.

Those distinctions may seem obvious, but they become increasingly important as the volume of AI-generated work grows.

Productivity Has a Hidden Cost

One of the most common arguments for AI agents is productivity.

And there is good reason to believe that agents can reduce the effort required for certain types of work.

But I think organizations need to be more careful about what they’re measuring.

Suppose an AI agent completes a task in 20 minutes that would normally require three hours.

That sounds like a significant efficiency improvement.

But what happens if the output requires an hour of review, another hour of correction, and additional time resolving unintended consequences?

The real benefit is considerably smaller.

Now imagine the agent completes ten similar tasks simultaneously.

Suddenly, the organization has more output, but potentially a much larger verification burden.

You may have accelerated production while creating a bottleneck in quality assurance.

This is why counting tasks completed, lines of code generated, or reports produced can be misleading.

Those measures describe activity.

They don’t necessarily describe value.

The more meaningful questions are:

  • How much useful work was completed correctly?
  • How much human intervention was required?
  • How frequently did work need to be corrected or repeated?
  • What was the total cost, including oversight?
  • Did the result improve the experience of customers, employees, or the business?

A hundred completed tasks mean very little if twenty need to be redone.

Real productivity is not how much work AI produces. It’s how much reliable work the organization can actually use.

Autonomy Should Be Earned, Not Assumed

We often discuss AI autonomy as though more autonomy automatically means greater progress.

I don’t think that’s the right starting point.

The appropriate level of autonomy should depend on the nature of the work, the reliability of the system, and the consequences of failure.

An agent identifying outdated documentation presents a different risk from an agent modifying production systems.

Drafting a customer response is different from sending that response.

Preparing a financial recommendation is different from executing a financial transaction.

These differences matter.

Organizations should establish clear boundaries for what an agent can do independently, what requires human approval, and what should remain under direct human control.

And those boundaries shouldn’t remain static.

As systems demonstrate reliability in specific workflows, organizations can expand their authority carefully.

When problems occur, authority may need to be reduced until the underlying issues are understood.

This is not fundamentally different from how effective leaders develop trust within their teams.

Trust is built through demonstrated performance, clear expectations, and accountability.

Autonomy without accountability isn’t empowerment. It’s unmanaged risk.

Who Owns the Mistake?

Imagine an AI agent makes an incorrect change that disrupts a customer-facing service.

The agent was following its instructions.

The person who assigned the task believed the scope was clear.

The automated tests passed.

And yet the service fails.

Who is responsible?

The person who assigned the work?

The individual who reviewed the results?

The technology leader who approved the deployment?

The executive who authorized the use of AI agents?

There may be multiple contributing failures, but the organization cannot assign responsibility to the software itself.

AI can participate in a workflow. It cannot accept organizational accountability in the way a human decision-maker can.

That is why responsibility needs to be established before execution, not reconstructed after something goes wrong.

For consequential work, someone should own the outcome, approval requirements should be explicit, and the organization should maintain enough visibility to understand what actions were taken.

Otherwise, the efficiency gained through automation can quickly disappear when teams are forced to investigate problems they cannot easily explain.

The principle is straightforward:

Delegating work to AI does not delegate accountability.

The Next Leadership Skill Is Orchestration

The leaders who benefit most from AI agents may not be those who automate the greatest number of tasks.

They may be those who learn to design effective systems of human and machine collaboration.

That requires a different set of management questions.

Rather than simply asking, “Can AI do this?” leaders should ask:

  • “Should AI be allowed to do this independently?”
  • “What would a successful outcome look like?”
  • “How will we know the result is correct?”
  • “What happens when the system encounters something unexpected?”
  • “And who has the authority to intervene?”

These are operating-model questions, not just technology questions.

They require business leaders, technology teams, risk owners, and frontline employees to establish shared expectations about how work gets done.

They also require organizations to become more disciplined about defining what completion actually means.

For too long, many businesses have confused being busy with being productive.

AI agents have the potential to magnify that problem.

A system capable of generating enormous amounts of activity can create the appearance of extraordinary progress, even when the work doesn’t contribute meaningfully to business outcomes.

The leader’s job is to distinguish between the two.

The Real Opportunity

I’m optimistic about what AI agents can make possible.

Smaller organizations may gain access to capabilities that previously required much larger teams.

Employees may spend less time on repetitive coordination and more time solving meaningful problems.

Technology teams may move from managing endless task queues toward designing and improving entire workflows.

But none of these benefits is automatic.

Simply adding agents to an organization doesn’t create a better operating model.

It can just as easily create faster processes, more complexity, and new forms of operational risk.

The organizations that succeed will need more than powerful AI tools.

They will need clarity about decision rights, reliable methods of verification, appropriate controls, and leaders willing to remain accountable for the results.

And perhaps most importantly, they will need to resist the temptation to mistake automation for organizational maturity.

A Final Thought

For years, technology leadership has focused on helping people work more efficiently through better systems.

AI agents are introducing something different.

We’re now building systems that can participate directly in the work itself.

That changes the role of management.

The question is no longer simply how to help employees become more productive.

It’s how to coordinate people, intelligent systems, and business processes so that the organization produces outcomes it can trust.

The technology will continue to improve.

Agents will become more capable. Workflows will become more sophisticated. And the amount of work that can be delegated will likely grow.

But one responsibility remains firmly human.

Someone still has to own the outcome.

And that’s why I believe AI agents won’t eliminate management.

They’ll change what good management looks like.

Signal vs. Noise explores the intersection of technology, leadership, and organizational change—with a focus on what actually creates value.

I’d be interested in hearing from other leaders: As AI agents begin taking on more work, what are you most concerned about—reliability, accountability, or knowing when to trust the results?
